readerTitle: Same 50-hour week. Why did only one manager finish the big job?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (물류창고 운영 책임자 vs 소프트웨어 회사 창업자, 식당, 앱 회사 엔지니어링 리드) + 실제 저술 (Drucker 1967, Paul Graham 2009 에세이)
insight: 시간 관리는 더 빨리 일하는 기술이 아니라, 급한 일이 몰려오기 전에 중요한 일의 자리를 먼저 정해 두는 일이다.
misconception: 바쁘게 많이 일하면 중요한 일도 결국 끝난다. 틈나는 시간을 모으면 큰 일도 할 수 있다.

sources.text: Drucker, P. F. (1967). The Effective Executive, chapter "Know Thy Time".
Graham, P. (2009). Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule.
Dana, Leo, 식당, 앱 회사 사례와 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Drucker는 『The Effective Executive』(1967) "Know Thy Time" 장에서 실제 시간 사용을 기록하라고 하고, 자유롭게 쓸 수 있는 시간을 큰 덩어리로 모으라고 권합니다. 조각난 시간은 합계가 많아도 충분하지 않다는 취지입니다. 카드 문구는 의역이니 원문과 대조해 확인하세요.
Paul Graham(2009) 에세이의 요지는 메이커에게 오후 중간의 회의 하나가 오후 전체를 망칠 수 있다는 것입니다. 회의가 오후를 너무 짧은 두 조각으로 나누기 때문입니다. 표현을 다시 확인하세요.
차트는 가상 수치입니다. Dana는 6 + 44 = 50시간, Leo는 0 + 50 = 50시간입니다. 2번 카드의 '약 6시간 필요'와 '3시간 오전 2번'(= 6시간)이 일치하는지 확인했습니다.
8번 카드의 회의 22개와 엔지니어 8명은 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Same 50-hour week. Why did only one manager finish the big job?
body: Dana runs a regional warehouse. Leo runs a small software company. Both worked about 50 hours last week, and both had one job that really mattered.
Dana finished hers. Leo answered over 200 messages, fixed a dozen small problems, and never started his.

image.label: Two busy desks: one with a finished plan, one buried in notes
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 화면을 반으로 나눔. 왼쪽은 창고 사무실 책상 위에 완성된 창고 배치도 한 장이 깔끔하게 놓여 있음. 오른쪽은 노트북 주변에 메시지 알림 말풍선과 포스트잇이 수북하고 가운데 빈 문서가 있음. 두 책상 위 시계는 모두 같은 시각. 실제 로고와 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You're Dana. Peak season is six weeks away.
body: You need to redesign the picking layout so orders move faster at peak. The job needs about six hours of real thinking. Your days are full of late trucks, staff questions and calls from the floor.
When does the layout work happen?

options.text: In the gaps between floor issues, whenever things go quiet
options.feedback: Staying available feels responsible. But quiet gaps are short and rare, and a layout redesign can't be done in ten-minute pieces.

options.text: After the shift ends, when the building is empty
options.feedback: You get focus, at the cost of long days you can't keep up through peak. It also teaches everyone that real work happens after hours.

options.text: Two three-hour mornings this week, with a supervisor covering the floor
options.feedback: The important job gets a fixed place before urgent work fills the week. The supervisor handles most issues, and only real emergencies reach you.

cards.title: Where the hours actually went
body: Dana blocked two mornings and handed floor issues to a supervisor. Leo kept his door and his chat open all week. He planned to start the pricing redesign "once things calm down." They never did.

rows.label: Focused time on the big job
Focused time on the big job

cards.title: Urgent vs important
body: **Urgent** work demands attention now: a late truck, a customer message, a bug report. **Important** work moves the business forward: a better layout, new pricing, a hiring plan.

Urgent work shouts. Important work waits quietly, so it loses every single day unless you decide in advance when it happens. Managing your time means placing the important work on the calendar first, then letting urgent work fill the rest.

image.label: A weekly calendar with two large blocks placed first
image.brief: 주간 캘린더 인포그래픽. 화요일·목요일 오전에 큰 진한 색 블록 두 개("Important work")가 먼저 놓여 있고, 그 주변 빈칸을 작은 연한 색 조각들("Calls", "Messages", "Issues")이 채움. 큰 블록이 먼저 자리 잡았다는 느낌이 들게.

cards.title: Big work needs big blocks.
body: In *The Effective Executive* (1967), Peter Drucker told managers to record where their time actually goes, because memory is a poor guide. He also urged them to gather their free time into large, unbroken blocks. Many small scraps of time, he argued, don't add up to serious work, even when the total looks impressive.
In a 2009 essay, programmer and investor Paul Graham made a similar point: for people doing deep work, one meeting in the middle of the afternoon can break up the whole afternoon.

cards.title: A block needs a rule for the noise.
body: Dana's mornings worked because of one clear rule. The supervisor handled everything except safety problems and major customer complaints. Without a rule like that, a block is just a hope.
The same works far from a warehouse. A restaurant owner reviews food costs every Monday from 9 to 11, before prep starts. Staff know that only a kitchen emergency interrupts.

image.label: Restaurant office door with a simple 'back at 11' sign
image.brief: 식당 뒤편 작은 사무실 문에 손글씨 메모 "Cost review until 11 · Kitchen emergencies only". 문 안쪽 책상에 영수증과 계산기. 따뜻한 조명. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.softwareNote: In a software team, the rule often looks like this: chat notifications off during the block, and one on-call teammate handles incidents and decides what is truly urgent.

cards.title: Not every role should block its time.
body: Some jobs exist to respond: a shift supervisor, a support agent, an on-call engineer. For them, being interruptible is the work. Blocking it away makes them a bottleneck.

Managers should protect a few blocks a week, not every hour. A manager who is never reachable slows the whole team. And when a real emergency breaks a block, let it. Then move the block. Don't delete it.

cards.title: Now it's an app company.
body: You lead a team of eight engineers. Your boss wants a written hiring plan for next year by Friday. Your calendar has 22 meetings this week, and chat pings every few minutes.

options.text: Decline or shorten a few meetings and block two half-days for the plan
options.feedback: You trade some availability for the one job only you can do. Tell the team who covers their questions during those blocks.

options.text: Write it in the 15-minute gaps between meetings
options.feedback: The minutes may add up, but a hiring plan needs connected thinking. Scattered pieces tend to produce a rushed, shallow draft.

options.text: Ask your boss to push the deadline back a week
options.feedback: Sometimes fair, but next week will likely look the same. Without protected time, a delay just moves the problem.

cards.title: Put the important work on the calendar first.
body: Urgent work will always find you. Important work only happens when you give it a fixed, protected place, with a clear rule for what may interrupt it.
**Try it today:** name one important job you keep postponing. Book a two-hour block for it this week, and tell one person what should wait until it's over.
